cards.title: Kermer and colleagues · expected and actual emotions after a coin flip
cards.aim: Do people predict their emotions after a win or a loss accurately?
cards.manipulated: Outcome of a coin flip: win an extra $5 or lose $3 (after being given $5). Predicted feelings (before the flip) were compared with actual feelings (after).
cards.measured: Happiness ratings: a baseline rating before the experiment, then predicted and actual changes from baseline.
cards.found: Before the flip, people expected losing $3 to drop happiness about 4 points and winning $5 to raise it about 2 points. After the flip, the real drop was about 1 point and the real rise about 1.2 points.
cards.means: People overestimate how bad a loss will feel, because they ignore their coping mechanisms; this feeds risk aversion.
cards.trap: The loss was the smaller amount of money ($3 vs $5) but was expected to hurt about twice as much as the gain helped.

cards.title: Simonsohn · cloudy days, admissions, and enrollment
cards.aim: Does the weather, an incidental factor, carry into important decisions?
cards.manipulated: Weather: cloudy vs sunny days (on the day of the admissions decision, or the day of the campus visit).
cards.measured: Admissions decisions (what was weighted) and whether visiting students enrolled.
cards.found: Simonsohn (2007): applicants' academic attributes were weighted more heavily on cloudy days than sunny days. Simonsohn (2009): visitors to a highly rated university were more likely to enroll if they visited on a cloudy day.
cards.means: Weather is an incidental factor that can change important decisions even though it is unrelated to the applicant or the school.
cards.trap: Do not mix up the two years: 2007 is admissions decisions, 2009 is enrollment by visitors.

cards.title: Lerner and colleagues · mood and highlighter prices
cards.aim: Can a mood unrelated to the decision change how much an object seems worth?
cards.manipulated: Film clip watched first: sad (a person dying), disgust (a person using a dirty toilet), or neutral (fish at the Great Barrier Reef).
cards.measured: Selling price and buying price for a set of highlighters.
cards.found: Selling: neutral about $4.50, disgust about $2.70, sad about $3.00. Buying: neutral about $3.50, disgust about $3.00, sad about $4.50.
cards.means: Incidental mood influences decisions: disgust lowered both prices, and sadness lowered selling but raised buying.
cards.trap: Sad lowers the selling price but RAISES the buying price; disgust lowers both.

cards.title: Physicians · earlier cases and cesarean recommendations
cards.aim: Does the context of earlier cases change a decision about the same case?
cards.manipulated: What came before the same test case: nothing (control), four serious-complication cases, or four fairly routine (not serious) cases.
cards.measured: Whether physicians recommended a cesarean section for the test case.
cards.found: Significantly more doctors recommended cesarean after reading the non-serious cases first.
cards.means: Context, including recently considered cases, changes how the same patient is judged.
cards.trap: The test case never changed; only the cases before it did.

cards.title: Organ donation · opt-in and opt-out consent
cards.aim: Does the way the choice is presented change how many people become organ donors?
cards.manipulated: Opt-in procedure (must take a step to be a donor) vs opt-out procedure (a donor unless you ask not to be).
cards.measured: Consent rate in countries using each procedure.
cards.found: Opt-in countries have under 28% consent; opt-out countries have over 99% consent.
cards.means: The status quo bias, the tendency to do nothing when a decision is difficult, makes the default decide the result.
cards.trap: Doing nothing means non-donor under opt-in but donor under opt-out.

cards.title: Tversky and Kahneman · the disease problem in gain and loss frames
cards.aim: Does describing the same outcomes as gains or as losses change risk-taking?
cards.manipulated: Frame: gain frame (A: 200 saved for certain; B: 1/3 chance all 600 saved, 2/3 chance none) vs loss frame (C: 400 die for certain; D: 1/3 chance no one dies, 2/3 chance all 600 die).
cards.found: Gain frame: 72% chose A (sure), 28% chose B. Loss frame: 78% chose D (gamble), 22% chose C.
cards.means: The framing effect: gains push people to risk aversion (sure thing), losses push them to risk taking (gamble), though A=C and B=D.
cards.trap: A and C are the same outcome, and B and D are the same gamble; only the wording changed.

cards.title: Sanfey and colleagues · the ultimatum game and the anterior insula
cards.aim: Do emotion and brain activity explain why people reject unfair offers that cost them money?
cards.manipulated: Offer size ($5/$5, $7/$3, $8/$2, $9/$1) and partner type (human vs computer); each participant played 20 games, 10 with each partner type.
cards.measured: Whether the responder accepted or rejected, plus activation of the right anterior insula.
cards.found: $5/$5 and $7/$3 were accepted almost always. $8/$2 was accepted about 53% (human) vs 85% (computer); $9/$1 about 37% (human) vs 68% (computer). More right anterior insula activation meant rejecting more offers.
cards.means: Emotion (anger at unfairness) is important in decision making; utility theory says accept any offer, but people do not.
cards.trap: Utility theory says accept any offer because any money beats nothing; rejecting costs both players.

cards.title: Belief bias · judging invalid believable conclusions
cards.aim: Does a believable conclusion make people accept a syllogism as valid?
cards.measured: Whether participants judged the syllogism valid.
cards.found: 71% judged invalid syllogisms with believable conclusions as valid.
cards.means: Belief bias: people judge by whether the conclusion sounds true instead of whether it follows.
cards.trap: Example: All of the students are tired / Some tired people are irritable / Some of the students are irritable sounds fine but is not valid.

cards.title: Conditional syllogisms · four forms and accuracy
cards.aim: Which kinds of if-then syllogisms do people judge correctly?
cards.manipulated: The four forms, all with If p, then q: p (modus ponens), not q (modus tollens), q, and not p.
cards.measured: Whether participants judged each form valid or invalid correctly.
cards.found: Modus ponens (valid) 97% correct; modus tollens (valid) 60%; syllogism 3 (invalid) 40%; syllogism 4 (invalid) 40%.
cards.means: Both valid forms were judged correctly more often than both invalid ones, but modus tollens is much harder than modus ponens even though both are valid.
cards.trap: Modus tollens is valid; syllogisms 3 and 4 are not.

cards.title: Wason four-card problem · abstract and concrete versions
cards.aim: Does using real-world items make conditional reasoning easier?
cards.manipulated: Abstract version (cards E, K, 4, 7; rule: vowel then even number) vs concrete version (cards Beer, Soda, 16 years old, 21 years old; rule: drinking beer then 21 years old).
cards.measured: Which cards participants chose to turn over.
cards.found: Abstract: 46% chose 4 (error), only 7% chose 7 (correct). Concrete: 73% answered correctly.
cards.means: Following the falsification principle, look for cases that break the rule; permission schemas in familiar rules make this easier.
cards.trap: Correct cards are E and 7 (abstract) and beer and 16 years old (concrete); the 4 and the 21 cannot break the rule.

existing_explainers.title: What a syllogism is and its parts
existing_explainers.plain: A syllogism is the basic form of deductive reasoning, introduced by Aristotle. It has two premises and a conclusion.
steps: 1. Find the two premises: the statements the reasoning starts from.
2. Find the conclusion: the third statement, what you arrive at.
3. Ask only one thing: does the conclusion follow from the two premises?
existing_explainers.example: Premise 1: All birds are animals. Premise 2: All animals eat food. Conclusion: Therefore, all birds eat food. Birds are inside animals, animals are inside things that eat food, so birds are inside that group too.
existing_explainers.watchOut: A categorical syllogism uses all, no, or some about two categories. Do not mix it up with the conditional syllogism, which starts with If p, then q.
explain: Deductive reasoning means working out whether a conclusion logically follows from some premises, where a premise is a statement that the reasoning starts from. The job is narrow. It does not ask whether the conclusion is likely or whether you happen to believe it, only whether it follows, and the answer is either yes or no with nothing in between.

A syllogism is the basic form of deductive reasoning, and it was introduced by Aristotle. It always has the same three-part shape: two statements called premises, which are what you are given, and a third statement called the conclusion, which is where the reasoning arrives and what you are asked to accept. The first move with any syllogism is simply to sort the statements into those two roles.

The first kind is the categorical syllogism, which describes how two categories relate to each other using the words all, no or some. With the premises All birds are animals and All animals eat food, the conclusion is Therefore, all birds eat food. It works because the category of birds sits completely inside the category of animals, and animals sit completely inside the category of things that eat food. If the smallest group is inside the middle one and the middle one is inside the largest, the smallest has to be inside the largest too.

Another case is all poodles are dogs and all dogs are mammals, so all poodles are mammals. It works like nesting boxes: poodles fit in a box labeled dogs, and the dogs box fits inside a bigger box labeled mammals. Because the first box is inside the second and the second is inside the third, the first is automatically inside the third, and you never have to inspect a single poodle. The conclusion is forced purely by how the boxes sit inside one another, and that is what deductive means: if the premises are true, the conclusion has no choice.

A categorical syllogism is different from a conditional syllogism, which begins with If p, then q instead of all, no or some. For either kind the single question is the same: given these two premises, does the conclusion have to follow?

existing_explainers.title: How to check validity, step by step
existing_explainers.plain: There is no easy method, so picture the situation the premises describe and try to break the conclusion (the mental model approach).
steps: 1. Build a picture (model) of the situation the two premises describe.
2. Write a tentative conclusion, one that might hold.
3. Look for an exception: a case where the premises are true but the conclusion is not.
4. If you find one exception, the syllogism is not valid. If no model of the premises refutes the conclusion, it is valid.
existing_explainers.example: All of the students are tired; Some tired people are irritable; so Some of the students are irritable. Everything sounds reasonable, but the conclusion does not follow from the premises, so the syllogism is not valid.
existing_explainers.watchOut: Do not stop at the first model that fits. A conclusion is valid only if NO model of the premises refutes it.
explain: There is no easy method for deciding whether a syllogism is valid, and it cannot be settled at a glance. What people do instead is picture the situation the premises describe, which is the idea behind the mental model approach of Johnson-Laird (1999). A mental model is one specific, concrete situation held in the mind that fits the premises, one way the premises could be true.

The procedure runs in a fixed order. You build a model of the situation, then write down a tentative conclusion, meaning a conclusion that might hold in that picture. The step people skip is the next one, which is to hunt for an exception, a way the premises could still be true while the conclusion is false. If even one model makes the premises true and the conclusion not true, the conclusion is refuted and the syllogism is not valid. It is valid only if no model of the premises can refute the conclusion.

The premises All of the students are tired and Some tired people are irritable, with the conclusion Some of the students are irritable, show how this works. Every student is among the tired people, but there are also tired people who are not students, and the second premise only says that some tired people are irritable without saying which ones. The irritable ones could all be non-students. Then both premises are true and no student is irritable, and that one exception is enough to make the syllogism not valid.

This is why every statement can sound reasonable and the syllogism can still fail. The word some leaves open which tired people are irritable, and being tired alone does not put any student among them. The danger is stopping at the first picture that fits, where the irritable people happen to be students, because a tentative conclusion often fits the first model built. Other ways the premises could be true have to be tried deliberately before the conclusion is trusted.

The same method works with cats. If all of my cats are hungry and some hungry animals are noisy, it sounds fine to conclude that some of my cats are noisy. But suppose the kitchen holds two cats and a dog, all hungry, with the dog as the only noisy one. Both premises hold and no cat is noisy, so the conclusion was never forced. If the second premise is instead all hungry animals are noisy, the conclusion that all my cats are noisy cannot be broken: every cat is hungry and every hungry animal is noisy, so no scene keeps the premises and escapes the conclusion. That is what validity looks like, a hard search for an exception in which every attempt fails.

existing_explainers.title: Validity versus truth
existing_explainers.plain: Valid means the conclusion follows from the premises. True means the statement matches the world. They are different.
steps: 1. Ignore whether the statements sound true.
2. Check only the form: does the conclusion follow from the two premises?
3. Then separately ask whether each statement is actually true.
4. Remember: valid plus true premises forces a true conclusion; valid with a false premise can give a false conclusion.
existing_explainers.example: All birds are animals; All animals have four legs; All birds have four legs. It has the same form as the first example, so it is valid. The conclusion is false only because premise 2 is false.
existing_explainers.watchOut: A syllogism can be invalid even if every statement and the conclusion seem reasonable (the students example). Valid does not guarantee a true conclusion.
explain: Valid and true are two different things. Valid describes the reasoning: a syllogism is valid if its conclusion follows logically from its two premises. True describes a statement and the world: does it match how things actually are? Validity depends on the form of the argument, while truth depends on whether the statements are correct, and confusing the two is what makes it hard to judge whether reasoning is logical.

All birds are animals, All animals eat food, so all birds eat food, and All birds are animals, All animals have four legs, so all birds have four legs, have exactly the same form, birds inside animals and animals inside a further group. Since the first has that form and its conclusion follows, the second does too, so both are valid.

What differs is the premises. In the first, both premises are true, so the conclusion is true as well. In the second, the claim that all animals have four legs is false, and that single false premise is the only reason its conclusion is false. So if a syllogism is valid and its premises are true, the conclusion must be true, but a valid form fed a false premise can still deliver a false conclusion. Validity alone does not guarantee a true conclusion.

Validity works like a well-built machine and truth like what is fed into it. A machine built so that all X are Y and all Y are Z always returns all X are Z. Feed it all the pets in my house are robots and all robots run on batteries, and out comes all the pets in my house run on batteries. The reasoning is valid, but the conclusion is false because my pets are not robots, so the bad input is to blame and not the machine. Feed it all poodles are dogs and all dogs are mammals and the true inputs give the true output, all poodles are mammals. A good machine plus true premises gives a true conclusion, and nothing beyond that.

Truth and validity also come apart in the other direction. In the students example, every statement sounds reasonable, yet the syllogism is not valid because the conclusion does not follow. Likewise All dogs are animals and Some animals are pets, so some dogs are pets, has only true sentences and is still not valid, because a world where the only pets are hamsters keeps both premises true and makes the conclusion fail. A true ending does not rescue weak reasoning. The skill is two separate passes: first ask only whether the conclusion follows from the premises, ignoring whether anything sounds true, and then separately ask whether the statements are true.

existing_explainers.title: Belief bias
existing_explainers.plain: Belief bias is thinking a syllogism is valid just because its conclusion is believable.
steps: 1. Notice if your gut says the conclusion is true.
2. Set that feeling aside.
3. Check whether the conclusion follows from the premises (look for an exception).
4. Judge validity from that, not from belief.
existing_explainers.example: 71% of participants judged invalid syllogisms with believable conclusions as valid. All of the students are tired; Some tired people are irritable; Some of the students are irritable sounds right but is not valid.
existing_explainers.watchOut: Good reasoning and truth are not the same thing; do not accept reasoning just because the ending sounds true.
explain: Belief bias is the tendency to think a syllogism is valid when its conclusion is believable. The ending matches what a person already thinks, it feels right, and the whole argument gets waved through without any check on whether it earns that ending.

This is common: 71% of participants judged invalid syllogisms with believable conclusions as valid, which is most people. Good reasoning and truth are not the same thing, and people make many errors in evaluation because of this, so the feeling that a conclusion sounds right is a warning and not evidence.

The syllogism All of the students are tired, Some tired people are irritable, therefore some of the students are irritable shows how it fools people. Each sentence sounds fine and the ending is easy to accept, since tired people being irritable is believable. But all the students are inside the group of tired people, and the second premise says only that some tired people are irritable, not which ones. The irritable ones could be entirely outside the students, making both premises true while no student is irritable. The conclusion does not follow, so the syllogism is not valid however believable it sounds.

A friend who says all of the cafe's pastries are sweet and some sweet things are bad for your teeth, so some of the cafe's pastries are bad for your teeth, gets a nod before the sentence is even finished, because sugary pastries are believed to be rough on teeth. That quick nod is belief bias. Tested properly, the premises can both be true with the pastries being soft fruit tarts that are gentle on teeth, while some hard candy elsewhere is sweet and bad for teeth. Then no pastry from the cafe is bad for teeth, so the conclusion was never forced even though it might well be true in real life.

The fix is a procedure and not a feeling. Register what your gut says about the conclusion, set it aside on purpose, and check whether the conclusion follows from the premises by looking for an exception. Validity is decided from that check and not from belief. A useful test is to imagine the very same shape with an ending you do not believe: if you would hunt for an exception then, hunt for one now. The pull toward a believable ending is a feeling about the world, while validity is about whether the conclusion follows, and sounding right is not the same as following.

existing_explainers.title: Conditional syllogisms: the four forms cheat sheet
existing_explainers.plain: All four start with If p, then q. p is the condition and q is what follows. They differ in the second premise.
steps: 1. Write the first premise as If p, then q.
2. Identify the second premise: p, not q, q, or not p.
3. Match it: p so q (valid); not q so not p (valid); q so p (not valid); not p so not q (not valid).
4. Valid forms: go forward from p, or backward from not q.
existing_explainers.example: If I study, I'll get a good grade. Form 1: I studied, so I'll get a good grade (97% correct). Form 2: I didn't get a good grade, so I didn't study (60%). Form 3: I got a good grade, so I studied (40%). Form 4: I didn't study, so I didn't get a good grade (40%).
existing_explainers.watchOut: Two are valid and two are not. Both valid types were judged correctly more often than both invalid ones.
explain: Conditional syllogisms are a second family, different from the all, no and some kind. They have two premises and a conclusion, and the first premise always has the form if p, then q, where p stands for a condition and q for what follows when that condition is met. In the running example the first premise is If I study, I'll get a good grade, so p is studying and q is getting a good grade. All four types start with that same sentence.

The four types differ only in the second premise and in what is concluded from it. In type 1 the second premise is p, I studied, and the conclusion is q, so I'll get a good grade. In type 2 the second premise is not q, I didn't get a good grade, and the conclusion is not p, so I didn't study. In type 3 the second premise is q, I got a good grade, and the conclusion is p, so I studied. In type 4 the second premise is not p, I didn't study, and the conclusion is not q, so I didn't get a good grade.

Types 1 and 2 are valid and types 3 and 4 are not. The valid types either confirm p or deny q, while the invalid types either confirm q or deny p. Put another way, the valid ones go forward from the condition or backward from a missing result, and the invalid ones are the reverse of that.

The rule if it rains, the ground is wet makes the pattern concrete, with p as it rains and q as the ground is wet. If it rains, the ground is wet, which is the forward direction. If the ground is dry, it cannot have rained, because rain would have left it wet, which is the backward direction. Those are the two valid forms. If the ground is wet, it did not necessarily rain, because a sprinkler or a spilled bucket would do the same. If it did not rain, the ground is not necessarily dry, for the same sprinkler reason. Both wrong forms fail because they treat the rule as if it also said that rain is the only way to a wet ground.

People's performance followed the logic only partly. Type 1 was judged correctly 97% of the time, type 2 only 60%, and types 3 and 4 only 40% each. Both valid forms were judged correctly more often than both invalid forms, but valid does not mean easy, which is why each pair needs to be understood on its own.

existing_explainers.title: Modus ponens and modus tollens (the valid ones)
existing_explainers.plain: Modus ponens: the condition is met, so the result follows. Modus tollens: the result did not happen, so the condition did not happen.
steps: 1. Modus ponens: If p, then q; p; therefore q.
2. Modus tollens: If p, then q; not q; therefore not p.
3. Test tollens in words: if studying always leads to a good grade, no good grade means no studying.
4. Both are valid with any content.
existing_explainers.example: If I study, I'll get a good grade. I didn't get a good grade. Therefore, I didn't study. Valid, though only 60% judged it correctly (vs 97% for modus ponens).
existing_explainers.watchOut: Modus tollens is just as valid as modus ponens, yet people find it much harder.
explain: Modus ponens and modus tollens are the two valid conditional forms, and each has a Latin name. The first premise is the same in both, If I study, I'll get a good grade, and only the second premise changes.

Modus ponens is the simple one. The second premise is I studied, so the condition is met, and the conclusion is Therefore, I'll get a good grade. In letters that is if p then q, p, therefore q. It moves forward, in the same direction as the rule: the studying happened, studying leads to a good grade, so the good grade has to follow. Nearly everyone gets this right, and 97% judged it correctly. A concert gate shows the same thing, since if you have a ticket you are let in, and a guard who sees you holding a ticket lets you through.

Modus tollens is the same rule used the other way round. The second premise is I didn't get a good grade, and the conclusion is Therefore, I didn't study. In letters that is if p then q, not q, therefore not p. If the studying had happened, a good grade would have had to follow, and there was no good grade, so the studying cannot have happened. At the concert gate, a person who was not let in cannot have had a ticket, because a ticket would have gotten them through, and this is known without ever seeing their pockets. A board game gives the same shape: if you roll a six, you move again, your friend did not move again, so they did not roll a six.

Modus tollens is exactly as valid as modus ponens, yet only 60% of participants judged it correctly against 97% for modus ponens. The reason is direction. Modus ponens runs along the rule, while modus tollens runs against it, from a result that did not happen back to a condition that did not happen, and reasoning backward from something absent is harder. The lower success rate does not make tollens shaky, because it is valid with any content and the difficulty lies in the people and not in the logic. The short version is that if the promised result is missing, the condition cannot have been there, because if it had been there the result would have followed.

existing_explainers.title: Why syllogisms 3 and 4 are not valid
existing_explainers.plain: If p, then q says what happens when p is true. It does not say q happens only then, and it says nothing about when p is false.
steps: 1. Syllogism 3 (q so p): the premise does not say studying is the only way to get a good grade.
2. Swap in other content to test it: If I live in Tucson, then I live in Arizona; I live in Arizona; so I live in Tucson fails.
3. Syllogism 4 (not p so not q): the premise says nothing about not studying, and a good grade could come another way.
4. If you can find a case where the premises hold but the conclusion fails, it is not valid.
existing_explainers.example: Syllogism 4: If I study, I'll get a good grade; I didn't study; therefore I didn't get a good grade. A person could get a good grade for some other reason, so the conclusion does not follow.
existing_explainers.watchOut: Only 40% got each of these right. The first premise does not support either conclusion.
explain: Once modus ponens and modus tollens are accepted as valid, it is tempting to think the other two directions work as well. They do not, because the first premise says less than it seems to. If p, then q tells what happens when p is true. It does not say that q happens only then, and it says nothing about what happens when p is false. Both invalid syllogisms come from reading more into the sentence than it contains.

Syllogism 3 has the premises If I study, I'll get a good grade and I got a good grade, and it concludes Therefore, I studied. This runs from the result back to the condition. The first premise says what happens when someone studies but never says that studying is the only way to get a good grade, so a good grade could have come from somewhere else and the conclusion does not follow. The same form with other content makes the flaw obvious: If I live in Tucson, then I live in Arizona. I live in Arizona. Therefore, I live in Tucson. A person can live in Arizona without living in Tucson.

Syllogism 4 has the premises If I study, I'll get a good grade and I didn't study, and it concludes Therefore, I didn't get a good grade. This runs from a missing condition to a missing result. The first premise says nothing about what happens when someone does not study, and a good grade could come about some other way. It is the same kind of error as syllogism 3, only from the other side. Only 40% judged each of these correctly, which makes sense because the conclusions feel natural while the first premise supports neither.

Any familiar rule shows it. If it is a golden retriever, then it is a dog. From it is a dog, it does not follow that it is a golden retriever, since it could be a beagle. From it is not a golden retriever, it does not follow that it is not a dog, since that same beagle is not a golden retriever and is still a dog. These are exactly the two invalid forms, with content that makes the flaw impossible to miss. The rule only says where golden retrievers end up, inside the dog group, and says nothing about the dog group containing only golden retrievers. When an invalid conclusion feels right, it is usually because the word only was quietly added to the rule, as in a cafe where if you show a student card you get a discount: someone with a discount may have used a coupon instead of a card, and someone with no card may still have gotten the discount through that coupon.

The test is the same one used throughout: can a case be found where the premises hold but the conclusion fails? If so, the form is not valid, and it is invalid wherever it appears. The first premise supports going forward from the condition and backward from a missing result, and nothing else.

existing_explainers.title: Mental models (Johnson-Laird, 1999) and the pool table
existing_explainers.plain: A mental model is a specific situation pictured in your mind that you use to judge a syllogism.
steps: 1. Create a model of the situation.
2. Generate tentative conclusions about the model.
3. Look for exceptions that falsify the model.
4. Decide validity from whether an exception exists.
existing_explainers.example: Pool table: a black ball directly above the cue ball, the green ball on the right of the cue ball, a red ball between them. The slide's answer is that the cue ball is to the left of the line of sight. Most people solve it by imagining the arrangement.
existing_explainers.watchOut: One model that fits the premises but not the conclusion is enough to reject the conclusion.
explain: Mental models answer the problem that there is no easy method for judging validity. People can imagine situations, so they can reason by picturing what the statements describe, and the pool table problem shows that they already do this.

In the pool table problem, a black ball is directly above the cue ball, the green ball is to the right of the cue ball, and a red ball is between them, meaning between the cue ball and the green ball. The speaker then moves so that the red ball is between the speaker and the black ball, and the question is which side of the speaker's line of sight the cue ball is on. Most people do not solve this with a rule. They imagine the arrangement: the black ball sits above the cue ball, the red ball and then the green ball lie off to its right, and from a spot where the red ball blocks the view of the black ball the cue ball sits off to the left. The answer is that the cue ball is to the left of the line of sight, reached by holding a picture in mind and not by applying a formula.

Johnson-Laird (1999) proposed that people use the same ability to solve deductive reasoning problems. A mental model is a specific situation represented in the mind, one concrete way the premises could be true. A person creates a model, generates tentative conclusions about it, and then looks for exceptions that would falsify it. A conclusion is valid only if no model of the premises can refute it, so a single model that fits the premises but not the conclusion is enough to reject the conclusion.

Three pets on a shelf make this ordinary. If the cat is to the left of the dog and the fish tank is to the right of the dog, picturing cat, dog, tank in a row shows the cat is to the left of the tank, with no rule needed. That little picture is a mental model, one concrete way the statements could be true.

A trickier version shows why exceptions matter. If the hamster is to the left of the dog and the fish tank is also to the left of the dog, the picture hamster, tank, dog suggests the hamster is to the left of the tank. But the arrangement tank, hamster, dog fits the same statements, and there the hamster is to the right of the tank. That single picture falsifies the tentative conclusion, because the statements never decided the order. In the first shelf puzzle every arrangement that can be built gives the same answer, which is why that conclusion holds up.

existing_explainers.title: The Wason four-card problem (abstract)
existing_explainers.plain: To test a rule, look for cards that could break it. This is the falsification principle.
steps: 1. Rule: if there is a vowel on one side, then there is an even number on the other.
2. Ask for each card: could its hidden side break the rule?

3. E: a non-even number behind it would break the rule, so turn it. K: not a vowel, cannot break it. 4: cannot break the rule whatever is behind it. 7: a vowel behind it would break the rule, so turn it.
4. Answer: turn E and 7.
existing_explainers.example: Cards E, K, 4, 7. 46% wrongly chose 4; only 7% chose the correct 7.
existing_explainers.watchOut: The 4 feels right because it fits the rule, but it cannot break the rule; most people fail to look for falsifying cases.
explain: The Wason four-card problem is a famous puzzle about testing a rule, and the natural response to it is the wrong one. Four cards show E, K, 4 and 7, and the rule is, if there is a vowel on one side, then there is an even number on the other side. The task is to decide the minimum number of cards that must be turned over to test the rule.

The falsification principle states that to test a rule, you must look for situations that falsify it, where to falsify a rule is to prove it false. The useful question is not which cards fit the rule but whether anything on a card's hidden side could break the rule. The E is a vowel, so an odd number behind it would break the rule, and it must be turned. The K is not a vowel, and the rule only speaks about what is behind vowels, so nothing behind K can break it. The 4 is even, and an even number fits the rule whether a vowel or a consonant is on the back, so nothing can break it. The 7 is odd, and a vowel on its other side would break the rule, so the 7 must be turned.

The correct answer is therefore E and 7. In the results, 46% of participants said the 4 needed to be turned over, which is an error, and only 7% said the 7 did, which is the correct choice. The 4 is tempting because an even number is what the rule seems to be about, and a vowel behind it would feel like a success, but a success that could not have been a failure tests nothing. Most participants fail to look for falsifying cases and look instead for evidence that agrees with the rule, which is why so few picked the 7.

The same logic applies to four cards with the rule if a card has a circle on one side, then the other side is blue, where what shows is a circle, a square, a blue card and a green card. The circle could break the rule if its back is any color other than blue, so it is turned. The green card could break it too, because a circle hiding on its back would be a circle with a non-blue side, exactly what the rule forbids. The square tells nothing, since the rule speaks only about circles. The blue card cannot hurt the rule, because a circle or a square behind it is fine, as the rule never said only circles may sit behind blue. So the circle and the green card are turned.

To test an if-then rule, then, look for the case that would break it, which here is a circle with no blue, and check only the cards that could be hiding that case: the circle itself and the card that is not blue.

existing_explainers.title: Concrete Wason version and permission schemas
existing_explainers.plain: A permission schema is the idea that if A is satisfied, B can be carried out. Familiar rules like a drinking age call it up and make the problem easier.
steps: 1. Rule: If drinking beer, then 21 years old.
2. Find the case that breaks it: someone drinking beer who is under 21.
3. Turn over beer (check the age) and 16 years old (check the drink).
4. Soda and 21 years old cannot break the rule.
existing_explainers.example: Cards Beer, Soda, 16 years old, 21 years old. 73% answered correctly. Being 21 is the condition; drinking beer is what can then be done.
existing_explainers.watchOut: The form is the same as the vowel rule. Familiarity is not always important, so the improvement does not come from familiarity alone; context that calls up a permission schema matters.
explain: The same puzzle becomes dramatically easier when it is stated in everyday terms. In the concrete version the rule is if drinking beer, then 21 years old, and the four cards read beer, soda, 16 years old and 21 years old. 73% of participants answered this version correctly, compared with 7% who found the 7 in the vowel version, so when the problem is stated in concrete everyday terms, correct responses greatly increase.

The same falsification question applies to each card: could its hidden side break the rule? The only case that breaks the rule is someone drinking beer who is under 21. The beer card must be turned, because the person's age might be under 21. The 16 years old card must be turned too, because the drink might be beer. The soda card cannot break the rule, since the rule says nothing about people drinking soda, and the 21 years old card cannot break it either, because someone who is 21 is allowed to drink anything. So beer and 16 years old are turned.

The explanation for the improvement is the permission schema, the idea that if A is satisfied, B can be carried out. A schema is a familiar pattern of knowledge, and a permission schema is the pattern of a rule that grants permission once a condition is met. In the beer rule, being 21 years old is the condition and drinking beer is what can then be carried out. People are familiar with rules like this, and the rule tells them exactly what to check: if someone is drinking beer, check their age, and if someone is 16, check what they are drinking. The abstract rule about vowels and even numbers does not call up this pattern, so people do not know what to look for.

A library shows the same thing. With the rule if someone is borrowing a book to take home, then they must have a library card, and four people at the desk, one showing a book, one reading at a table, one holding a card and one with no card, the person carrying a book out the door must be checked for a card, and the person with no card must be checked for a book. The reader at the table breaks nothing, because the rule never limited reading, and the person with a card breaks nothing, because a card holder may borrow or not borrow. This is a permission rule, a condition that must be met before an action is allowed, and the cheating to look for is the action without the permission.

The logical form is identical to the vowel and even number puzzle, so the logic did not change. What changed is that the rule matched a familiar pattern and told people what to check. Two cautions apply. Context is important, because the same problem becomes easier in a familiar setting, but familiarity is not always important, so familiarity alone does not explain the improvement. What helps is a context that brings up a permission schema.

existing_explainers.title: Framing effect: gain versus loss
existing_explainers.plain: The same facts worded as gains or as losses change what people choose.
steps: 1. Gain frame (saved): sure option vs gamble; people avoid risk.
2. Loss frame (die): sure option vs gamble; people take the risk.
3. Check that A equals C (200 saved = 400 die) and B equals D (same gamble).
4. Conclude that only the wording changed.
existing_explainers.example: 600 people at risk. A: 200 saved for certain (72% chose it); B: 1/3 chance all saved, 2/3 none. C: 400 die for certain (22%); D: 1/3 nobody dies, 2/3 all die (78%).
existing_explainers.watchOut: It is a switch in strategy caused by wording alone, not a difference in the outcomes.
explain: The framing effect is the finding that decisions are influenced by how a decision is stated. The wording of a choice can highlight one aspect of the situation, such as what might be gained or what might be lost, and the facts can stay exactly the same while the wording changes what people focus on. Tversky and Kahneman (1981) studied how framing changes the amount of risk people accept. When situations are framed in terms of gains, people tend toward a risk-aversion strategy, preferring the sure option. When they are framed in terms of losses, people tend toward a risk-taking strategy, preferring the gamble.

The disease problem shows this. A disease is expected to kill 600 people, and two programs have been proposed. In the gain frame the outcomes are described in terms of people saved. Program A: 200 people will be saved for certain. Program B: a 1/3 probability that 600 people will be saved and a 2/3 probability that no people will be saved. 72% of people chose Program A, the sure option, and 28% chose Program B, so most people avoided the risk even though the gamble could save everyone.

In the loss frame the same disease is expected to kill 600 people, but the outcomes are described in terms of people who will die. Program C: 400 people will die for certain. Program D: a 1/3 probability that no one will die and a 2/3 probability that 600 people will die. This time 78% of people chose Program D, the gamble, and 22% chose Program C.

The two versions are the same choice. If 200 of 600 people are saved, then 400 die, so Program C has the same outcome as Program A, and Program D is the very same gamble as Program B. Only the wording changed, yet most people switched from the sure option to the gamble. A statement about lives saved points to what can be gained, while a statement about deaths points to what can be lost, and that shift in attention is what moved people.

A pizza party with ten slices that might be ruined by a leaky oven shows the same structure. Plan one: five slices will be saved for certain. Plan two: a half chance that all ten are saved and a half chance that none are. Plan three: five slices will be ruined for certain. Plan four: a half chance that none are ruined and a half chance that all ten are ruined. Five saved for certain means five ruined, so plans one and three are the same plan, and a half chance of saving all ten is a half chance of ruining none, so plans two and four are the same gamble. Four plans make only two real options, and the framing effect predicts a lean toward the sure option under the saving wording and toward the gamble under the ruining wording.

The wording does this because saved points attention at what you keep, and a sure thing feels good, while ruined points attention at what you lose, and a sure loss feels worse than a chance of dodging it, so the gamble looks more attractive. The pizza case is an illustration of the pattern and not a result from any study. The facts stay the same, the words change, and the choice changes with them, so the switch comes from the wording and not from the outcomes.

qa_facts.q: How do emotions shape decisions, and what are expected emotions?
qa_facts.a: Emotions take part in decision making and do not only get in its way. People with damage to an area of their prefrontal cortex who have flattened emotions have impaired decision making. Anxious people tend toward risk avoidance, passing up choices that could lead to large negative consequences, and optimistic people ignore negative information and focus on positive information, which in excess can lead to poor decisions. Expected emotions are the emotions people predict they will feel about an outcome, and they are one determinant of risk aversion. People inaccurately predict their emotions, believing a particular loss will have a greater impact than a gain of the same size.

qa_facts.q: What did Kermer and colleagues (2006) find when they compared expected and actual emotions?
qa_facts.a: Kermer and colleagues (2006) gave participants $5 and told them a coin flip would win them another $5 or lose them $3, after rating their baseline happiness. Beforehand they expected losing $3 to lower happiness by about 4 points and winning $5 to raise it by about 2, so the expected loss was about twice the expected gain. Afterward the actual drop from losing was only about 1 point and the rise from winning about 1.2. People overestimated the negative feeling because they do not consider the coping mechanisms that get activated and soften a loss.

qa_facts.q: What are incidental emotions, and what did Simonsohn (2007, 2009) find about the weather?
qa_facts.a: Incidental emotions are emotions not specifically related to the decision, such as those from a person’s general disposition, a recent experience or the surroundings, like the weather. Simonsohn (2007) analyzed university admissions decisions and found applicants’ academic attributes were weighted more heavily on cloudy days than sunny days. Simonsohn (2009) found that prospective students visiting a highly rated university were more likely to enroll if they had visited on a cloudy day. The weather is unrelated to the applicants or the school but still changed the decision.

qa_facts.q: What did Lerner and colleagues (2004) find about mood and buying and selling prices?
qa_facts.a: In Lerner and colleagues (2004), participants watched a sad clip of a person dying, a disgust clip of a person using a dirty toilet, or a neutral clip of fish at the Great Barrier Reef, and then set a selling price and a buying price for highlighters. For selling, neutral was about $4.50, disgust about $2.70 and sad about $3.00. For buying, neutral was about $3.50, disgust about $3.00 and sad about $4.50. Disgust lowered both prices, while sadness lowered the selling price and raised the buying price. The clips were unrelated to the choice, so these were incidental emotions, and they changed how much the same object seemed worth.

qa_facts.q: How does the context of a decision and the way choices are presented matter, using the cesarean case and the opt-in versus opt-out donor rates?
qa_facts.a: Decisions depend on context. Physicians saw the same hypothetical cesarean test case in three contexts, alone first as the control, after four other cases with serious complications, or after four fairly routine cases. Significantly more doctors recommended cesarean after reading the non-serious cases first, so the cases just considered changed how the same patient was judged. Decisions also depend on how choices are presented. In opt-in countries a person must take an active step to be an organ donor, and consent rates are below 28 percent, while in opt-out countries a person is a donor unless they request otherwise, and consent rates are over 99 percent. The status quo bias is the tendency to do nothing when faced with a difficult decision, and since doing nothing leaves a person a non-donor under opt-in and a donor under opt-out, the rates end up far apart. The story The International Community shows a choice of the same kind, where the birds can only pick the sauce they are eaten with, not whether they are eaten.

qa_facts.q: What is the framing effect, and what did Tversky and Kahneman (1981) find in the disease problem?
qa_facts.a: The framing effect is when decisions are influenced by how a decision is stated, even when the facts are the same. Tversky and Kahneman (1981) found that gain framing leads to risk aversion, preferring the sure option, and loss framing leads to risk taking, preferring the gamble. In the disease problem, 600 people are expected to die. In the gain frame, Program A saves 200 for certain and Program B has a 1/3 chance that 600 are saved and a 2/3 chance that none are saved, and 72 percent chose A and 28 percent chose B. In the loss frame, Program C means 400 die for certain and Program D has a 1/3 chance that no one dies and a 2/3 chance that 600 die, and 78 percent chose D and 22 percent chose C. Program C is the same outcome as A, since saving 200 of 600 means 400 die, and D is the same gamble as B, so only the wording changed and the majority switched from the sure option to the gamble. A risk-aversion strategy avoids an uncertain outcome in favor of a certain one, and a risk-taking strategy accepts uncertainty in the hope of avoiding a certain loss.

qa_facts.q: What is neuroeconomics, and how does the ultimatum game used by Sanfey and colleagues (2003) work? What is the rational decision for the responder?
qa_facts.a: Neuroeconomics combines psychology, neuroscience and economics. Psychology contributes how people think and decide, neuroscience contributes what happens in the brain, and economics contributes how choices about money and value are analyzed. One finding is that decisions are influenced by emotions that are associated with activity in specific brain areas. In the ultimatum game used by Sanfey and colleagues (2003), a proposer gets $10 and offers the responder a split. The responder accepts, and the money is divided as offered, or rejects, and neither player receives anything. According to utility theory, the rational decision for the responder is to accept any offer, because even $1 is worth more than the nothing that comes from rejecting.

qa_facts.q: What did Sanfey and colleagues (2003) find about unfair offers, human versus computer partners, and the anterior insula?
qa_facts.a: In Sanfey and colleagues (2003), participants played 20 games, 10 with human partners and 10 with computer partners. Offers of $5 and $5 and of $7 and $3 were accepted almost every time, about 100 percent and about 95 percent for both partner types. Lower offers separated the partners. An $8 and $2 offer was accepted about 53 percent of the time from a human and about 85 percent from a computer, and a $9 and $1 offer was accepted about 37 percent from a human and about 68 percent from a computer. Participants often rejected low offers because they became angry that the offers were unfair, and they were less angry with an unfair computer. Participants with more activation of the right anterior insula, an area connected with emotional states, rejected more offers, even though rejecting meant getting nothing. So emotion is important in decision making, and it can lead people to give up money.

qa_facts.q: What are deductive reasoning, a syllogism and validity, and how is validity different from truth? What is belief bias?
qa_facts.a: Deductive reasoning is determining whether a conclusion logically follows from premises, which are the statements the reasoning starts from. A syllogism, introduced by Aristotle, has two premises and a conclusion, and a categorical syllogism describes the relation between two categories using all, no or some, such as All birds are animals, All animals eat food, therefore all birds eat food. A syllogism is valid if its conclusion follows logically from its premises, and if the premises of a valid syllogism are true then the conclusion must be true. Validity depends on the form of the reasoning while truth depends on whether the statements match the world. All birds are animals, all animals have four legs, therefore all birds have four legs is valid because it has the same form, but the conclusion is false only because the second premise is false. Syllogisms can also be invalid even though every statement seems reasonable, such as All of the students are tired, some tired people are irritable, some of the students are irritable. Belief bias is the tendency to think a syllogism is valid if its conclusion is believable, and 71 percent of participants judged invalid syllogisms with believable conclusions as valid.

qa_facts.q: What is the answer to the pool table problem, and what is the mental model approach (Johnson-Laird, 1999)?
qa_facts.a: There is a black ball directly above the cue ball, the green ball is to the right of the cue ball, and a red ball is between them. The speaker moves so the red ball is between the speaker and the black ball, and the cue ball is to the left of the line of sight. Most people solve it by imagining how the balls are arranged on the table, which is the basis of Johnson-Laird’s (1999) proposal that people use mental models for deductive reasoning. A mental model is a specific situation represented in a person’s mind to help determine the validity of syllogisms. The person first creates a model of the situation described by the premises and generates tentative conclusions, then looks for exceptions to falsify the model, a case where the premises are true but the conclusion is not, and finally determines validity from whether an exception was found. A conclusion is valid only if it cannot be refuted by any model of the premises, so if even one model fits the premises but not the conclusion, the conclusion does not follow.

qa_facts.q: What are the four conditional syllogisms, and why are modus ponens and modus tollens valid?
qa_facts.a: Conditional syllogisms have a first premise of the form If p, then q, and p is the condition and q is what follows. The four types differ in the second premise. Syllogism 1 goes from p to therefore q, syllogism 2 from not q to therefore not p, syllogism 3 from q to therefore p, and syllogism 4 from not p to therefore not q. Two are valid and two are not. Syllogism 1 is modus ponens. If I study I’ll get a good grade, I studied, therefore I’ll get a good grade. Since the condition is met, what follows from it has to follow too, and 97 percent of participants judged it correctly. Syllogism 2 is modus tollens. If I study I’ll get a good grade, I didn’t get a good grade, therefore I didn’t study. If studying always leads to a good grade, missing the grade means the studying did not happen. It is just as valid as modus ponens, yet only 60 percent judged it correctly.

qa_facts.q: Why are conditional syllogisms 3 and 4 not valid, and how often did people judge them correctly?
qa_facts.a: Syllogism 3 is If I study I’ll get a good grade, I got a good grade, therefore I studied. It is not valid because the first premise says what happens when someone studies, but it does not say studying is the only way to get a good grade. The same form with different content is If I live in Tucson then I live in Arizona, I live in Arizona, therefore I live in Tucson, where it is easier to see that a person can live in Arizona without living in Tucson. Syllogism 4 is If I study I’ll get a good grade, I didn’t study, therefore I didn’t get a good grade. It is not valid because the first premise says nothing about what happens when someone does not study, so a person could get a good grade for another reason. Only 40 percent judged each of these correctly, compared with 97 percent and 60 percent for the two valid types, so both valid types were judged correctly more often than both invalid types.

qa_facts.q: What is the Wason four-card problem, which cards should you turn over, and what is the falsification principle?
qa_facts.a: In the Wason four-card problem, four cards read E, K, 4 and 7, and the task is to find the minimum number of cards to turn over to test the rule If there is a vowel on one side, then there is an even number on the other side. The answer is to turn over the E and the 7. A 7 with a vowel on its other side would break the rule, so turning it over is a real test, and a 4 cannot break the rule whatever is on its back. 46 percent of participants chose the 4, which is an error, and only 7 percent chose the 7. The falsification principle states that to test a rule you must look for situations that falsify it, meaning prove it false, and most participants fail to do this. When the problem is stated concretely, with the rule If drinking beer, then 21 years old and cards reading Beer, Soda, 16 years old and 21 years old, 73 percent answered correctly. The cards to turn over are beer and 16 years old, because someone drinking beer while under 21 is the only case that breaks the rule.

qa_facts.q: What is a permission schema, and why does it make the card problem easier?
qa_facts.a: A permission schema is the idea that if A is satisfied, B can be carried out. A schema is a familiar pattern of knowledge, and a permission schema is the pattern of a rule that grants permission once a condition is met, such as a drinking age. It is used in the concrete versions because people are familiar with rules of this kind, so a permission rule is easier to reason about than an abstract rule about letters and numbers. In the beer version, being 21 is the condition that must be satisfied and drinking beer is what can then be carried out. Context is important, because the same logical problem becomes easier in a familiar setting that calls up a permission schema. Familiarity is not always important, so the improvement does not come from familiarity alone.
